THOUGHT: This 54-year-old male presents with a subacute, progressive triad of gait disturbance (now wheelchair-dependent), urinary incontinence, and dysarthria — often referred to as the “classic triad” of multiple system atrophy (MSA). Additional supportive features include parkinsonism (rigidity, mild tremor, bradykinesia inferred from inability to perform rapid alternating movements), cerebellar signs (implied by gait ataxia and dysarthria—though not explicitly labeled as ataxic speech, slurring in MSA is commonly mixed spastic-ataxic or hypokinetic; MRI shows cerebellar and brainstem atrophy), autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic hypotension without compensatory tachycardia on autonomic testing, plus urinary incontinence), and absence of red flags for mimics (e.g., no fever/infection, normal urinalysis rules out UTI-related delirium or cystitis, no visual changes or seizures to suggest paraneoplastic or inflammatory etiologies). The MRI findings — atrophy and signal changes in brainstem, cerebellum, and basal ganglia — are highly characteristic of MSA (particularly MSA-P [parkinsonian] or MSA-C [cerebellar] subtypes; here, rigidity dominates but cerebellar involvement is evident on imaging and clinically via gait and speech). Age of onset (54) is typical for MSA (mean ~60, but range 30–80; early-onset cases occur). Parkinson disease typically lacks prominent early autonomic failure and cerebellar atrophy. Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) may cause gait instability and dysarthria but usually spares autonomic function early and shows midbrain atrophy (“hummingbird sign”), not cerebellar/pons atrophy. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) can present with gait apraxia, incontinence, and cognitive slowing—but speech is spared, rigidity/tremor/orthostatic hypotension are absent, and MRI would show ventriculomegaly without brainstem/cerebellar atrophy. Lewy body dementia is less likely given absence of fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, or REM sleep behavior disorder, and prominent early autonomic and cerebellar signs are atypical. The combination of sporadic, adult-onset, progressive parkinsonism + cerebellar signs + autonomic failure + neuroimaging evidence of multisystem neurodegeneration strongly points to MSA.

DIAGNOSIS: Multiple system atrophy
